passage:
Tuesday night.

Signed the form today. Economics honours. It's official, no more "maybe biology, maybe design, maybe law" every week.

Bhupen asked me at lunch, "Aadhya, why so pale?" Honestly, I was scared. Choosing one thing means letting the others go. I kept thinking of the plant-cell diagrams I used to love, and my sketchbook from Class 11.

But when I sat in that economics intro class last month, the lecturer explained why onion prices jump every year and something clicked. I stayed back for an hour asking questions. I haven't felt that curious in ages.

So yes. Economics. I'll keep drawing for myself. Maybe I'll mix it in somehow later.

Mummy cried a little on the phone. Happy tears, I think. I'm still a bit wobbly but mostly excited. 😊

qa.q: What subject did Aadhya sign up for?
qa.a: Economics honours.

qa.q: Why was Aadhya scared when signing the form?
qa.a: Committing to economics meant letting go of other interests Aadhya loved, like biology and drawing.

qa.q: What would you advise Aadhya while settling into the course?
qa.a: Keep following the curiosity that made Aadhya stay back after class, and keep drawing on the side so that part isn't lost.

qa.q: How might Bhupen see Aadhya's choice?
qa.a: Bhupen noticed the pale face, so may be concerned but also glad Aadhya finally made a decision after swinging every week.

grounding: A young adult's diary shows a student committing to a specific major and the mixed feelings that come with it.

passage:
Vandana: I did it. I enrolled at the ITI for the electrician course.
Sunaina: WAIT. what about the BA seat??
Vandana: I let it go. I sat through 3 weeks of BA classes and felt nothing
Vandana: then I helped my uncle rewire his shop and it was like my brain lit up
Sunaina: that's actually amazing
Sunaina: how did your parents take it
Vandana: Mummy is worried people will talk. "a girl climbing poles"
Vandana: Papa just said "if you're sure, finish it properly"
Sunaina: are you sure?
Vandana: yes. scared but yes
Vandana: two years, then apprenticeship. I want my own electrical business one day
Sunaina: then I'm your first customer. my fan has been making noises for a month 😅
Vandana: deal. after I pass the safety module 🙂
Sunaina: proud of you 💪

qa.q: What course did Vandana enroll in at the ITI?
qa.a: The electrician course.

qa.q: How does Vandana feel about her decision?
qa.a: She is scared but certain, because working on the wiring made her feel alive in a way the BA classes never did.

qa.q: How could Vandana's mother be supported with her worries?
qa.a: Vandana could share what she learns and her business plan, and maybe introduce her to women already working in the trade.

qa.q: How might Sunaina's reaction affect Vandana?
qa.a: Sunaina's excitement and joke about being the first customer help Vandana feel backed and less alone in an unusual choice.

grounding: Shows through a chat a young woman committing to a vocational trade path over a general degree.

passage: In the village, most boys Yogesh's age were leaving for city jobs. His cousin Ojas had gone to Mumbai and sent back photos of tall buildings. Yogesh, nineteen, stood at the edge of his father's sugarcane field one evening with the admission letter for a two-year agriculture diploma at the district college. His father had struggled for years with failing crops and falling water. Yogesh had seen the drip irrigation at the model farm on the highway and couldn't stop thinking about it. "You want to study farming?" his father asked, half laughing. "Papa, I want to learn how to farm better," Yogesh said. That night, he signed the form by lantern light, his heart thumping, and folded it into his shirt pocket for the morning bus.

qa.q: What did Yogesh see at the model farm on the highway?
qa.a: Drip irrigation.

qa.q: What does Yogesh's thumping heart show when he signs the form?
qa.a: He is nervous but determined, committing to a path different from the other boys and from what his father expected.

qa.q: How could Yogesh's father support his choice?
qa.a: He could share his own farming experience and let Yogesh try new ideas on a small part of the field as he learns.

qa.q: Why might Ojas react differently to Yogesh's choice?
qa.a: Having left for the city, Ojas may see farming as the old life, while Yogesh sees it as a future he can improve.

grounding: Shows a young man in a village committing to a specialised agricultural path to build a future on the family land.

passage: In the laundry room of her residence in Montreal, Rania, nineteen, held the form due on Friday: declare your major. She had taken intro psychology, economics and an art elective, and liked them all a little. Her roommate Camila folded towels beside her. 'Which one made you forget to eat?' Rania thought. It wasn't any of the classes. It was her weekend job at the bike co-op, rebuilding wheels, where three hours felt like ten minutes. 'That's not a major.' 'The college has a mechanical technology program,' Camila said. 'Two years. Hands-on.' Rania's stomach flipped: fear of disappointing her parents, and something like relief. That night she emailed the program advisor. On Friday she handed in the form with a new name written in.

qa.q: When was the form due?
qa.a: On Friday.

qa.q: What mix of feelings did Rania have when Camila mentioned the program?
qa.a: She felt afraid of disappointing her parents and also relieved, as if a real fit had been named.

qa.q: What could Rania do to feel surer about her choice?
qa.a: She could talk with the advisor and current students, and explain her reasons to her parents calmly.

qa.q: How might Rania's parents react to her new path?
qa.a: They might be surprised or worried at first, but could come round if they see how committed and happy she is.

grounding: Shows a young adult committing to a specific hands-on program after noticing where her real absorption lies.

passage: The electrical workshop at the ITI smelled of hot solder and dust. Kiran, twenty, finished wiring the practice board and flicked the switch; all four bulbs lit. Vijay Sir, the instructor, nodded but didn't smile. 'Your cousins are all doing BCom, no?' 'Yes, sir.' 'And you?' Kiran wiped his hands. For a year he had been half in, half out, thinking he might switch to a degree once the relatives stopped asking. 'I want the wireman licence,' he said. 'Then solar installation. I'm not switching.' He was surprised how steady his voice sounded. Vijay Sir finally smiled and handed him the form for the advanced solar module. 'Then stop coming late on Mondays.' Kiran laughed. 'Yes, sir.'

qa.q: How many bulbs lit when Kiran flicked the switch?
qa.a: All four.

qa.q: What did Kiran notice about his own voice, and what does it show about how he felt?
qa.a: He was surprised it sounded steady, which shows he felt sure of his choice after a year of doubt.

qa.q: How did Vijay Sir support Kiran's commitment?
qa.a: He gave him the form for the advanced module and also held him to a standard about punctuality.

qa.q: How might Kiran's relatives see his choice?
qa.a: Some may compare him with the cousins doing BCom, but they may come to respect a skilled trade.

grounding: Illustrates a young adult committing to a specific trade path at a training institute.
